topic: Measure: capability, performance and sigma metrics

notes.front: What does process capability compare?
notes.back: The output of an in-control process with its specification limits, using capability indices.
notes.explanation: The comparison is a ratio: the width the specification allows against the width of the process, measured as six process standard deviations.
notes.example: Like checking whether a van fits through a gate: the gate is the specification, the van's width is the spread of the process.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Process capability compares the output of an in-control process to the specification limits by using capability indices . The comparison is made by forming the ratio of the spread between the process specifications (the specification "width") to the spread of the process values, as measured by 6 process standard deviation units (the process "width").

notes.front: How is the capability index Cp calculated?
notes.back: Cp = (upper specification limit − lower specification limit) ÷ 6σ: the specification width over the process width.
notes.explanation: The denominator is six process standard deviations, the process "width", so a bigger Cp means the specification has more room for the process spread.
notes.example: Like a 10 cm slot for parts whose spread covers 5 cm: the slot is twice the spread, a ratio of 2.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: The comparison is made by forming the ratio of the spread between the process specifications (the specification "width") to the spread of the process values, as measured by 6 process standard deviation units (the process "width").

image.alt: A bell-shaped process distribution sits between a lower specification limit (LSL) on the left and an upper specification limit (USL) on the right. An arrow between the two limits is labelled specification width = USL − LSL. A shorter arrow under the curve, from the mean minus 3σ to the mean plus 3σ, is labelled process width = 6σ. Below, the formula reads Cp = (USL − LSL) / 6σ.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6

notes.front: How is the capability index Cpk calculated?
notes.back: The smaller of (upper specification limit − mean) ÷ 3σ and (mean − lower specification limit) ÷ 3σ.
notes.explanation: Taking the minimum means Cpk is set by whichever specification limit the mean sits closer to.
notes.example: Like judging a car in its lane by the gap to the nearer kerb, not by the width of the lane.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain

notes.front: What is defects per unit (DPU)?
notes.back: The total number of defects counted, divided by the number of units produced.
notes.explanation: Every defect found goes into the count, so one unit with several faults adds several defects to the total.
notes.example: Like marking essays: 12 spelling mistakes across 4 essays is 3 per essay, however they are spread.
notes.source: LeanOhio, “Lean Six Sigma Terminology” (ver. 2), “Defects Per Unit (DPU)”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is defects per million opportunities (DPMO), and how is it calculated?
notes.back: Defects per million chances for a defect to occur: total defects ÷ total opportunities × 1,000,000.
notes.explanation: It is the figure that a sigma conversion table turns into a sigma level.
notes.example: Like counting typing errors per million keystrokes rather than per document.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Six Sigma Conversion Table”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is first pass yield (FPY)?
notes.back: The percentage of units that meet specification without any rework or repair.
notes.explanation: A unit counts only if it was right first time; a unit that had to be fixed along the way does not.
notes.example: Like the share of learner drivers who pass at their first attempt, with no retest.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Lean Six Sigma and Process Improvement Metrics Definitions”, “First Pass Yield”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On MoreSteam's sigma conversion table, what does yield mean?
notes.back: The percentage of units produced correctly, with no defects, at the first attempt.
notes.explanation: The page gives a yield beside the DPMO for sigma levels 3 to 6, so the two measures can be read together.
notes.example: Like the share of loaves that come out of the oven fit to sell.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Six Sigma Conversion Table”, “What is Yield?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is rolled throughput yield (RTY)?
notes.back: The probability that a process with more than one step turns out a defect-free unit.
notes.explanation: It judges the process as a whole, across all its steps, rather than any single step.
notes.example: Like the chance that a parcel comes through every hand-off in a delivery chain undamaged.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Rolled throughput yield” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: in production economics is the probability that a process with more than one step will produce a defect free unit.

notes.front: What is a process's sigma level?
notes.back: A statistical estimate of how many defects the process will produce, matched to its defects per million opportunities.
notes.explanation: It puts the same performance that DPMO counts onto a different scale.
notes.example: Like turning a count of complaints into a star rating.
notes.source: LeanOhio, “Lean Six Sigma Terminology” (ver. 2), “Sigma Level”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the 1.5 sigma shift built into the sigma conversion table?
notes.back: An allowance for the process drifting by 1.5 standard deviations over time.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam's reason is that processes tend to show instability of about that size as time passes, so the table assumes it.
notes.example: Like leaving extra following distance on a motorway because speeds creep up and down.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Six Sigma Conversion Table”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Most capability index estimates are valid only with a large enough sample, generally thought to be about {{c1::50}} independent data values.
notes.explanation: Below about 50 values the estimates are not treated as valid, and the same page adds that capability studies generally need at least 100.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Most capability indices estimates are valid only if the sample size used is "large enough". Large enough is generally thought to be about 50 independent data values.

notes.front: The Cp, Cpk and Cpm statistics assume that the population of data values is {{c1::normally distributed}}.
notes.explanation: The handbook states this assumption for all three indices together, just before it defines them.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: statistics assume that the population of data values is normally distributed.

notes.front: How does the handbook express Cpk in terms of Cp?
notes.back: Cpk = Cp(1 − k), where k is the scaled distance between the process mean and the midpoint of the specification range.
notes.explanation: When the mean sits exactly on the midpoint, the distance k is zero and Cpk equals Cp.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: can also be expressed as \(C_{pk} = C_p(1-k)\), C pk = C p (1-k), --> where \(k\) k --> is a scaled distance between the midpoint of the specification range, \(m\), m , --> and the process mean

notes.front: Cpk can never be {{c1::greater than}} Cp; the two are equal when the process is centred on its nominal value.
notes.explanation: Cpk combines Cp with a term for how far the mean sits from the middle of the specification, which Cp leaves out.
notes.source: LeanOhio, “Lean Six Sigma Terminology” (ver. 2), “Cpk”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When a specification has only one limit, which capability indices does the handbook use?
notes.back: Cpu = (upper specification limit − mean) ÷ 3σ, or Cpl = (mean − lower specification limit) ÷ 3σ.
notes.explanation: Each one sets the spread allowed on one side of the mean against the actual spread on that side.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: $$ C_{pu} = \frac{\mbox{allowable upper spread}} {\mbox{actual upper spread}} = \frac{\mbox{USL} - \mu} {3\sigma} $$ --> and $$ C_{pl} = \frac{\mbox{allowable lower spread}} {\mbox{actual lower spread}} = \frac{\mu - \mbox{LSL}} {3\sigma} \, , $$

notes.front: In the handbook's table translating capability into rejects, what reject rate goes with Cp = 1.00?
notes.explanation: The process spread uses 100% of the specification width; like every figure in the table, it assumes the process is centred in the specification.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: 1.00 1.33 1.66 2.00 Rejects 0.27 % 64 ppm 0.6 ppm 2 ppb % of spec used 100 75 60 50

notes.front: In the handbook's table translating capability into rejects, what reject rate goes with Cp = 1.33?
notes.back: About 64 ppm (parts per million).
notes.explanation: The process spread uses 75% of the specification width; the handbook's reject figures assume the process is centred in the specification.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: 1.00 1.33 1.66 2.00 Rejects 0.27 % 64 ppm 0.6 ppm 2 ppb % of spec used 100 75 60 50

notes.front: In the handbook's table translating capability into rejects, what reject rate goes with Cp = 2.00?
notes.back: 2 ppb (parts per billion).
notes.explanation: The process spread uses only half (50%) of the specification width; the handbook's reject figures assume the process is centred in the specification.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: 1.00 1.33 1.66 2.00 Rejects 0.27 % 64 ppm 0.6 ppm 2 ppb % of spec used 100 75 60 50

notes.front: LeanOhio's glossary equates Six Sigma with a Cp of {{c1::2.0}}.
notes.explanation: The same glossary describes Cp as running from zero upwards, with a larger value meaning a more capable process.
notes.source: LeanOhio, “Lean Six Sigma Terminology” (ver. 2), “Cp”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What Cpk does MoreSteam give as the goal, and what higher threshold does it say many industries use?
notes.back: A Cpk above 1.0; many industries use 1.33.
notes.explanation: Below 1.0, MoreSteam says, the process may not be able to meet its specification consistently.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “The Process Capability Index (Cpk)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two remedies the handbook lists for capability analysis when the process data are not normal?
notes.back: Transform the data to near-normal (for example Box-Cox); use indices built for non-normal distributions.
notes.explanation: Of the transformations, the handbook names Box-Cox as a popular one.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Transform the data so that they become approximately normal. A popular transformation is the Box-Cox transformation - Use or develop another set of indices, that apply to nonnormal distributions.

notes.front: On what should the number of opportunities in DPMO be based, and what does inflating it do?
notes.back: On critical-to-quality characteristics; inflating the count lowers the defect ratio and pushes the sigma level up.
notes.explanation: A defect is a failure to meet a characteristic customers care about, so only those characteristics are real chances for a defect.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Lean Six Sigma and Process Improvement Metrics Definitions”, “Defects Per Million Opportunities (DPMO)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two reasons MoreSteam calls first pass yield a measure of dubious value?
notes.back: Rework and repair are often hidden, done up the line but not recorded; several defects on one unit are not captured.
notes.explanation: Defects per unit avoids the second problem, since it counts every defect found on every unit.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Lean Six Sigma and Process Improvement Metrics Definitions”, “First Pass Yield”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Rolled throughput yield is the {{c1::product}} of the yields of every step in the process.
notes.explanation: Multiplying the step yields is how the measure captures the cumulative effect of losses throughout the process.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Rolled throughput yield” (CC BY-SA 4.0)
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: It is the product of yields for each process step of the entire process. [ 2 ] For any process, it is ideal for that process to produce its product without defects and without rework. Rolled throughput yield quantifies the cumulative effects of inefficiencies found throughout the process.

notes.front: On MoreSteam's sigma conversion table, what DPMO and yield go with a three-sigma process?
notes.back: About 66,800 DPMO, a yield of 93.32%.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam labels three sigma moderate quality, well short of the six-sigma target.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Six Sigma Conversion Table”, “What Do Sigma Levels Indicate?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On MoreSteam's sigma conversion table, what DPMO and yield go with a four-sigma process?
notes.back: Roughly 6,210 DPMO, a yield of 99.38%.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam calls four sigma good quality. Its 6,210 DPMO is roughly a tenth of the 66,800 at three sigma.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Six Sigma Conversion Table”, “What Do Sigma Levels Indicate?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On MoreSteam's sigma conversion table, what DPMO and yield go with a five-sigma process?
notes.back: About 233 DPMO, a yield of 99.977%.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam rates five sigma as excellent quality, one step below the six-sigma target.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Six Sigma Conversion Table”, “What Do Sigma Levels Indicate?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On MoreSteam's sigma conversion table, what DPMO and yield go with a six-sigma process?
notes.back: 3.4 DPMO, a yield of 99.99966%.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam names this level as the target for Six Sigma projects.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Six Sigma Conversion Table”, “What Do Sigma Levels Indicate?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A filling line's specification runs from 490 g to 510 g, and its process standard deviation is 2.5 g. What is Cp?
notes.choicesExplained: B divides the 20 g specification width by 12σ instead of 6σ. C divides by 4σ. D divides by 2σ.
notes.explanation: Cp sets the specification width (20 g) against the process width of six standard deviations (15 g): 20 ÷ 15 = 1.33.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: The comparison is made by forming the ratio of the spread between the process specifications (the specification "width") to the spread of the process values, as measured by 6 process standard deviation units (the process "width").

notes.front: The same filling line (specification 490 g to 510 g, standard deviation 2.5 g) now runs with a mean of 504 g. What is Cpk?
notes.choicesExplained: C is the lower-side value, (504 − 490) ÷ 7.5; Cpk takes the smaller side. B is Cp, which ignores where the mean sits. D divides the 6 g gap by 6σ instead of 3σ.
notes.explanation: The upper side gives (510 − 504) ÷ 7.5 = 0.80 and the lower side 1.87; Cpk is the minimum of the two.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain

notes.front: A supplier reports Cp = 1.33 and quotes “about 64 ppm rejects” from the handbook's table, but its process mean sits well off the centre of the specification. What is wrong with the quote?
notes.choices:
A) The table's reject figures assume a process centred in the specification
B) 64 ppm belongs to Cp = 2.00, not 1.33
C) Cp cannot be 1.33 when the mean is off centre
D) The table applies only to one-sided specifications
notes.back: A: the reject figures assume a centred process.
notes.choicesExplained: B: the table gives 2 ppb for Cp 2.00; 64 ppm is right for 1.33. C: Cp compares widths only, so an off-centre mean does not change it. D: the table is built on two limits, upper and lower.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives its reject figures only for a distribution centred in the specification, so they do not describe an off-centre process.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: where ppm = parts per million and ppb = parts per billion. Note that the reject figures are based on the assumption that the distribution is centered at

notes.front: Call-handling times at a contact centre are strongly right-skewed, and a manager wants a capability index against the 10-minute limit. Which step fits the handbook's advice?
notes.choices:
A) Transform the data towards normality (such as Box-Cox), or use an index built for non-normal data
B) Delete the longest calls so the data look normal
C) Report the median instead of any index
D) Calculate Cpk as usual; the index does not depend on the data's shape
notes.back: A: transform the data, or use a non-normal index.
notes.choicesExplained: D: the usual indices assume normally distributed data. B: dropping real data is not one of the handbook's remedies. C: the handbook's remedies still produce a capability measure; they do not abandon it.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists transforming the data and using indices for non-normal distributions among its remedies.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Transform the data so that they become approximately normal. A popular transformation is the Box-Cox transformation - Use or develop another set of indices, that apply to nonnormal distributions.

notes.front: A coating process's control chart shows several points out of control. A manager asks for its Cpk today. Which reply fits the handbook's definition of capability?
notes.choices:
A) Report Cpk now; the index allows for instability
B) Report Cp instead, because Cp ignores where the process is centred
C) Report Cpk, but from twice as much data
D) Hold off: capability compares the output of a stable, in-control process with its specification
notes.back: D: capability is defined for a stable, in-control process.
notes.choicesExplained: A: the definition starts from an in-control process; the index does not adjust for instability. B: Cp rests on the same in-control definition. C: more data from an unstable process does not make it stable.
notes.explanation: The handbook's comparison is between the output of a stable process and its specification, which this process is not yet.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.6 “What is Process Capability?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: We are often required to compare the output of a stable process with the process specifications and make a statement about how well the process meets specification.

notes.front: A batch of 10 grant application forms is checked. There are 4 errors in all, and they are on just 2 of the forms. How many defects and how many defectives?
notes.choices:
A) 4 defects and 2 defectives
B) 10 defects and 2 defectives
C) 4 defects and 4 defectives
D) 2 defects and 4 defectives
notes.back: A: 4 defects and 2 defectives.
notes.choicesExplained: D swaps the two terms. B counts every form as a defect. C treats each error as its own defective form, but the errors sit on only 2 forms.
notes.explanation: Each error is a defect; a form carrying one or more errors is a defective unit.
notes.source: LeanOhio, “Lean Six Sigma Terminology” (ver. 2), “Defect” and “Defective”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A clinic audits 80 referral letters and finds 20 defects in total. What is the defects per unit?
notes.choicesExplained: B divides units by defects, the wrong way round. C is a share of defective letters, which the audit does not give, since several defects may sit on one letter. D scales to a million, as DPMO would, and ignores opportunities.
notes.explanation: DPU divides all the defects found (20) by the number of units checked (80).
notes.source: LeanOhio, “Lean Six Sigma Terminology” (ver. 2), “Defects Per Unit (DPU)”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An assembly cell builds 400 units, each with 5 opportunities for a defect, and finds 12 defects. What is the DPMO?
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the opportunities and divides by units only. C is the defects per opportunity, 12 ÷ 2,000, not scaled to a million. D is the defects per unit, not scaled to a million opportunities.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Six Sigma Conversion Table”, “How Do You Calculate Sigma Level?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A billing process runs at about 6,210 DPMO. Using MoreSteam's conversion table, with its 1.5 sigma shift, what sigma level is that?
notes.choices:
A) 3 sigma
B) 4.5 sigma
C) 6 sigma
D) 4 sigma
notes.back: D: 4 sigma.
notes.choicesExplained: A goes with about 66,800 DPMO. B is the statistical tail distance behind 3.4 DPMO, not a table row for 6,210. C goes with 3.4 DPMO.
notes.explanation: The table pairs about 6,210 DPMO, or a 99.38% yield, with four sigma.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Six Sigma Conversion Table”, “What Do Sigma Levels Indicate?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Cp versus Cpk: which one ignores where the process is centred, and which standard deviation does MoreSteam's Cpk formula use?
notes.back: Cp ignores centring, as it assumes a centred process; MoreSteam's Cpk uses the within-subgroup standard deviation.
notes.explanation: Cp compares only spread with the specification range, while Cpk measures from the actual centre to the nearest limit.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “The Process Capability Index (Cpk)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For 3.4 defects per million opportunities, how far from the mean to the nearest limit do statistical tables put it, and what target does Six Sigma set instead?
notes.back: 4.5 standard deviations; the target is raised to 6.0 to allow for the process shifting over time.
notes.explanation: The gap of 1.5 between the two figures is exactly the shift the sigma conversion table assumes.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Six Sigma Conversion Table”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Defect versus defective: what is the difference?
notes.back: A defect is any one thing the customer would not accept; a defective is a whole unit carrying at least one defect.
notes.explanation: One defective unit can hold several defects, so counting defects and counting defectives can give different totals.
notes.source: LeanOhio, “Lean Six Sigma Terminology” (ver. 2), “Defect” and “Defective”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
